content: Lead (Pb) possesses four stable isotopes: 204Pb, 206Pb, 207Pb, and 208Pb. Additionally, it has one commonly encountered radiogenic isotope, 202Pb, which has a half-life of approximately 53,000 years. Lead is the heaviest element known to have a stable isotope. The isotopes of lead that arise within the radioactive decay chains of actinium, radium, and thorium are historically referred to by specific names: 206Pb is known as radium G. 207Pb is referred to as actinium D. 208Pb is called thorium D. 210Pb is known as radium D, radio-lead, or radiogenic lead. 211Pb is referred to as actinium B. 212Pb is called thorium B. 214Pb is known as radium B. The isotope 206Pb represents the terminal product of the uranium/radium decay series originating from uranium-238 (U-238). Similarly, 207Pb is the final product of the actinium decay series derived from uranium-235 (U-235). Lastly, 208Pb is the endpoint of the thorium decay series originating from thorium-232 (Th-232). Notes: The evaluated isotopic composition applies to most, but not all, commercially available samples. Variations in isotopic abundances and atomic mass limit the precision of these measurements. The provided ranges are generally applicable to normal terrestrial materials. There are geologically exceptional samples in which the isotopic composition falls outside the reported range. For such specimens, the uncertainty in atomic mass may exceed the stated value. Values marked with a are not solely derived from experimental data but are partially based on systematic trends. Spins with weak assignment arguments are enclosed in parentheses. Uncertainties are presented in concise form within parentheses following the corresponding last digits. These uncertainty values represent one standard deviation, except for isotopic composition and standard atomic mass values from IUPAC, which use expanded uncertainties.
